page.title: Proximal particle Langevin: theorems and source comparison
page.heading: Proximal interacting particle Langevin algorithms
page.subtitle: Proximal minimization, parameter-error estimates, and mean-field integral comparisons with their precise assumptions.
page.description: Mathematical proofs for proximal particle algorithms, including qualified versions of arXiv:2406.14292v3 results and explicit limitations.
page.status: The MYIPLA, PIPGLA, and MYPGD estimates relative to the original marginal maximizer stated here are proved under their specified assumptions. Their constants and some norms differ from the source, whose full set of claims is not established.
page.source_intro: The reference is arXiv:2406.14292v3. The corresponding formal statements are shown below, with differences in assumptions, constants, and conclusions stated explicitly.

intro:
The arguments concern Cordero Encinar, Crucinio and Akyildiz, Proximal Interacting Particle Langevin Algorithms, arXiv:2406.14292v3. The results below give finite-time parameter-error estimates for the specified MYIPLA, PIPGLA, and MYPGD recursions and finite-horizon mean-field comparisons.

The complete paper is not formalized. The proved estimates retain square-root smoothing displacement, explicit step-dependent gradient constants, and a finite stationary-coupling coefficient where they differ from the source. The statements identify their assumptions, target laws, and norms. Algebraic corrections and remaining source claims are recorded separately from these qualified theorems.

sections.title: Theorems and source qualifications
sections.intro: The source is version 3 of Proximal Interacting Particle Langevin Algorithms. Its PIPGLA target and gradient-scaling calculation differ from version 1. All comparisons and page references below concern version 3 unless another version is explicitly named.

steps.title: The proved results and their qualifications
steps.body:
The results below prove qualified versions of the source’s particle-convergence claims. Proximal minimizers and their envelopes are defined by global minimization. The Gaussian recursions have finite moments, and the MYIPLA, PIPGLA, and MYPGD bounds concern the original nonsmooth marginal maximizer under their stated assumptions.

The MYIPLA smoothing displacement has square-root order, obtained from a finite potential gap rather than the source’s Taylor-based linear claim. The PIPGLA proof uses a stationary synchronous coupling and a finite coefficient independent of the forward step. Positive proximal scales are compared by a proved sensitivity bound; the source’s heat-flow proof and exact constants are not reproduced. Scalar estimates conditional on a recurrence are distinguished from the recurrence derived for the splitting transition.

The mean-field force has a quadratic-Wasserstein regularity bound. The continuous mean-field integral equations, finite smoothing comparison, and independent-copy particle comparison are proved in timewise mean-square norm, with tagged one-time Wasserstein error of inverse-square-root particle order. These conclusions do not assert the source’s exact Appendix B formula, expected path-supremum estimates, or partial differential equations. The source comparison records separately algebraic counterexamples, missing arguments, and weaker proved results.

steps.title: The MYIPLA bound about the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Let \(U=g_1+g_2\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\). Assume \(g_1\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\) and \(L_1\)-Lipschitz gradient. Assume \(g_2\) is finite, convex, bounded below, and \(K\)-Lipschitz. For \(\lambda>0\) put

\[ V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda,\qquad L_\lambda=L_1+\lambda^{-1}. \]

Take \(N>0\), finite-second-moment initialization, mutually independent standard Gaussian innovations independent of initialization, and

\[ 0<\gamma\le\frac{2}{m+L_\lambda}. \]

Let \(\mu_n\) be the scaled MYIPLA law, \(\Pi_{\lambda,N}\) the smoothed Gibbs law, and \(\theta_\star\) a maximizer of \(\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx\). Then

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}} +\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+(1-m\gamma)^n W_2(\mu_0,\Pi_{\lambda,N})\\ &+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma. \end{aligned} \]

Normalization, stationary comparison, finite transport moments, and sharp equilibrium concentration follow from the preceding transport and particle results. The last term depends on \(\lambda\). The source’s claimed \(O(\lambda)+O(\lambda^2)\) smoothing expression is replaced here by the proved finite \(O(\sqrt\lambda)\) bound; the statement is therefore a qualified version of that source theorem.

Apply the smoothed-model estimate at \(\theta_\eta\) and use its finite second moment in

\[\bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_U\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\le\bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}+\|\theta_\eta-\theta_U\|.\]

The decomposition \(\theta_n-\theta_U=(\theta_n-\theta_\eta)+(\theta_\eta-\theta_U)\) gives this inequality by Minkowski. The deterministic term is bounded by the center comparison. Hence the four contributions are smoothing, equilibrium concentration, initial transport, and discretization. The coefficient still contains \(L_1+1/\eta\), so the admissible step and smoothing scale remain coupled.

sections.title: Convex proximal minimization
sections.intro: For finite convex potentials, the quadratic-penalized minimization problem gives a unique proximal point. Its residual support, nonexpansiveness, and envelope derivatives are derived from minimization. The assumptions include the finite-valued globally Lipschitz regime used in the main estimates; extended-valued indicator constraints in some source experiments are not covered here.

steps.title: Existence and uniqueness of the minimizer
steps.body:
For \(\lambda>0\) define

\[ Q_{\lambda,x}(p)=g_2(p)+\frac{\|p-x\|^2}{2\lambda},\qquad P_\lambda(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_p Q_{\lambda,x}(p). \]

A finite convex function is continuous in finite dimension. Under \(g_2\ge b\) the quadratic term forces \(Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\) above competitor value \(Q_{\lambda,x}(x)=g_2(x)\) outside a closed ball. Radius \(\sqrt{2\lambda(g_2(x)-b)}+1\) suffices. Compact attainment gives a minimizer inside the ball, and the outside estimate makes it global. The residual characterization implies uniqueness.

The formal definition assigns zero where existence has not been established. Every theorem used here assumes the convexity, lower bound, and positive \(\lambda\) that prove existence, so that auxiliary convention is never used in these conclusions.

steps.title: The residual characterizes the minimum
steps.body:
A vector \(s\) supports \(g_2\) at \(p\) when \(g_2(p)+\langle s,y-p\rangle\le g_2(y)\) for every \(y\). For positive proximal parameter, minimization is equivalent to the residual support condition

\[ p=P_\lambda(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{x-p}{\lambda}\in\partial g_2(p). \]

For necessity, compare the objective at a minimizer \(p\) with its value at \(p+t(y-p)\). Convexity bounds the function increment, and division by positive \(t\) followed by a limit gives the support inequality. For sufficiency, substitute that support in the difference of the quadratic objectives. The remaining squared norm is nonnegative, proving global minimality without differentiability of \(g_2\).

Monotonicity applied to the two residual supports gives

\[ \|P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\|^2 \le\langle x-y,P_\lambda(x)-P_\lambda(y)\rangle. \]

Cauchy–Schwarz proves nonexpansiveness of \(P_\lambda\). Expansion of the residual squared difference proves nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\). To state the necessity calculation explicitly, fix competitor \(y\) and put \(d=y-p\). Compare the objective at \(p\) and \(p+td\) for \(0<t\le1\). Convexity bounds \(f(p+td)\) by \((1-t)f(p)+tf(y)\). Expansion of the quadratic and division by \(t\) gives

\[f(y)-f(p)\ge\left\langle\frac{x-p}{\lambda},d\right\rangle-\frac{t}{2\lambda}\|d\|^2.\]

Letting \(t\downarrow0\) proves the support. Conversely the same support gives \(Q_{\lambda,x}(y)-Q_{\lambda,x}(p)\ge\|y-p\|^2/(2\lambda)\) at \(p\), quantitatively bounding the objective increase away from \(p\). Thus the support condition proves both optimality and quadratic growth of the penalized objective.

sections.title: Moreau envelope regularity
sections.intro: MYIPLA smooths the summand \(g_2\), producing \(g_1+g_2^\lambda\). PIPULA smooths the entire potential to \(U^\gamma\). These operations have different curvature and gradient constants, which are derived separately.

steps.title: Nonexpansiveness and the derivative
steps.body:
Define \(g_2^\lambda(x)=Q_{\lambda,x}(P_\lambda(x))\) and \(r_\lambda(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-P_\lambda(x))\). The residual support gives the lower comparison and the old minimizer as competitor gives the upper comparison:

\[ 0\le g_2^\lambda(y)-g_2^\lambda(x) -\langle r_\lambda(x),y-x\rangle \le\frac{\|y-x\|^2}{2\lambda}. \]

The upper remainder is little-o of \(\|y-x\|\), so \(\nabla g_2^\lambda=r_\lambda\). The global supports also give convexity. Nonexpansiveness of \(I-P_\lambda\) yields

\[ \|\nabla g_2^\lambda(x)-\nabla g_2^\lambda(y)\| \le\lambda^{-1}\|x-y\|. \]

For \(y=x+h\), the remainder divided by \(\|h\|\) is bounded by \(\|h\|/(2\lambda)\), which tends to zero. Thus the Fréchet derivative is \(h\mapsto\langle r_\lambda(x),h\rangle\). The residual-map inequality gives gradient Lipschitz constant \(1/\lambda\), hence continuity of the gradient. These facts justify smooth Langevin analysis for the envelope even when the original function is nonsmooth.

steps.title: The uniform Moreau value-gap estimate
steps.body:
If \(g_2\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz, the proximal residual support gives \(\|r_\lambda(x)\|\le K\) and hence \(\|x-P_\lambda(x)\|\le\lambda K\). The envelope value satisfies

\[ 0\le g_2(x)-g_2^\lambda(x)\le\frac{\lambda K^2}{2}. \]

Competitor \(x\) proves nonnegativity of the gap. For \(d=\|P_\lambda(x)-x\|\), value Lipschitzness bounds the gap by \(Kd-d^2/(2\lambda)\). Completing the scalar square gives maximum \(\lambda K^2/2\). The estimate is uniform over \(x\) and therefore implies \(V_\lambda\le U\le V_\lambda+\lambda K^2/2\). Exponentiation and latent integration preserve the finite comparison used below for marginal centers, without a Hessian or an integrated Taylor remainder.

sections.title: The particle update maps
sections.intro: Use scaled state \(z=(\theta,x^1/\sqrt N,\ldots,x^N/\sqrt N)\), pair extraction \(J_i z=(\theta,x^i)\), and summed potential \(\mathcal V_\lambda(z)=\sum_iV_\lambda(J_i z)\). Coordinate evaluation gives the update identities. After Gaussian distributions and independence are imposed, these same identities identify the finite-time probability laws.

steps.title: The pairwise residual and scaled Euler identity
steps.body:
For pair map \(P\), apply \(P\) to each \(J_i z\), average their parameter components, and divide their physical latent components by \(\sqrt N\). The state retains one common parameter rather than \(N\) independently evolving parameters.

For \(P=P_\lambda\) and smoothed potential \(V_\lambda=g_1+g_2^\lambda\), the residual-gradient formula gives

\[ \operatorname{Pair}_P(z)=z-\frac\lambda N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_2^\lambda(J_i z)\right). \]

Substitution into MYIPLA cancels the additional multiples of \(z\) and yields

\[ z_{n+1}=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\mathcal V_\lambda(z_n) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_n. \]

The parameter Gaussian coefficient is \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) and the physical latent coefficient is \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). Initialization and successor updates agree, so induction gives equality of all finite recursions. These are deterministic update identities before distributions or convergence estimates are imposed.

steps.title: The order of drift, proximity, and noise
steps.body:
PIPGLA first takes the noisy gradient step for \(g_1\) and then applies the pairwise proximal map:

\[ y_n=z_n-\frac\gamma N\nabla\!\left(\sum_i g_1(J_i z_n)\right) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\xi_n, \qquad z_{n+1}=\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(y_n). \]

PIPULA is the MYIPLA specialization with \(g_1=0\) and \(\lambda=\gamma\), in which proximity precedes the added Gaussian perturbation. The expanded MYIPLA update is

\[T_{\mathrm{MY}}(z,\xi)=(1-\gamma/\eta)z-\frac\gamma N\nabla F_{g_1}(z)+\frac\gamma\eta\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\xi.\]

In MYIPLA the pairwise proximal value is evaluated at the preceding state and contributes through an explicit residual drift. In PIPGLA it is evaluated at the already perturbed smooth step. These compositions give different outputs for the same innovation. Their update identities must therefore be proved separately. In the source convergence analysis PIPGLA is compared with the original nonsmooth Gibbs model; the MYIPLA theorem cannot be applied merely by changing the update’s name.

sections.title: MYIPLA convergence for the smoothed model
sections.intro: The residual identity makes the expanded MYIPLA recursion equal to Gaussian IPLA for the smoothed pair potential. Its derived curvature and gradient constants satisfy the transport theorem’s hypotheses. Sharp marginal concentration and parameter projection then give the bound relative to the smoothed marginal maximizer for the algorithm laws.

steps.title: The smoothed parameter-error estimate
steps.body:
Add the convex envelope to the \(m\)-strongly convex function \(g_1\). The sum retains modulus \(m\), and its gradient constant is \(L_\lambda=L_1+1/\lambda\). The identity \(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2\) gives full-state curvature \(Nm\), gradient constant \(NL_\lambda\), and dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\). Gaussian ULA at step \(\gamma/N\) therefore gives contraction \((1-m\gamma)^n\) and discretization term

\[ \frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\lambda}{m} \sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma. \]

The physical restriction \(\gamma\le2/(m+L_\lambda)\) is precisely the scaled ULA restriction. The prescribed Gaussian independence and finite initial moments give the required probability laws and finite transport. The parameter error at any fixed center belongs to \(L^2\). For smoothed marginal maximizer \(\theta_\eta\) and Gibbs target \(\Pi_{N,\eta}\), sharp concentration and projection give

\[\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\eta\|^2\right)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\eta})+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\eta}{m}\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma.\]

The general statement applies to any convex differentiable envelope with the residual-gradient identity and gradient constant \(\eta^{-1}\). For the Moreau envelope these properties are proved separately. The equilibrium radius is \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\), and the discretization coefficient depends on \(L_\eta/m\). Cancellation of \(N\) gives the physical step restriction. Thus particle count reduces equilibrium spread, but choosing a smaller smoothing scale also increases the gradient constant and restricts the step. The stationary reference and target moments are derived in the Gaussian transport theorem.

steps.title: Sharp concentration of the parameter marginal
steps.body:
For continuous \(a\)-strongly convex potential \(f\) with minimizer \(x_\star\), the dilation argument gives

\[ \int\|x-x_\star\|^2\,\pi(dx)\le\frac d a, \qquad\pi(dx)\propto e^{-f(x)}dx. \]

Only continuity, strong convexity, and a minimizing point are needed; no nonsmooth integration-by-parts formula is assumed. Prékopa–Leindler gives strong convexity of the parameter marginal potential. Raising the marginal likelihood to its \(N\)-th power multiplies that curvature by \(N\). Thus

\[ W_2(\Pi_{\lambda,N}^{\theta},\delta_{\theta_{\lambda,\star}}) \le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}. \]

This is the factor in the source’s equilibrium estimate. The earlier radius \(\sqrt{2d_\theta/(Nm)}\) was a valid weaker bound.

The parameter density is proportional to \(M(\theta)^N\) and has negative log potential \(NF(\theta)\). Its curvature is \(Nm\), with minimizer \(\theta_*\). The sharp theorem in dimension \(d_\theta\) gives \(\int\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2d\Pi_N\le d_\theta/(Nm)\). In the equivalent notation, density \(e^{-N\Phi}\) has curvature \(Nm\), so dimension \(d_\theta\) gives second moment \(d_\theta/(Nm)\). The exact projection identity transfers that same moment to the full Gibbs law; its nonnegative square root is the equilibrium root mean square radius.

sections.title: The original marginal maximizer
sections.intro: The original potential may be nonsmooth. Its comparison with a smooth strongly convex potential gives an integrable Gaussian majorant and a uniform finite value gap. Dominated convergence and parameter decay prove existence of the original marginal maximizer, and the negative log marginal comparison bounds its displacement without differentiating the original marginal.

steps.title: Marginal-potential comparison from a uniform gap
steps.body:
Suppose \(U\) is continuous and \(V\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(m>0\), and assume \(V\le U\le V+\delta\). Exponentiation reverses order, and integration over each latent fiber gives

\[ e^{-\delta}k_V(\theta)\le k_U(\theta)\le k_V(\theta), \qquad k_W(\theta)=\int e^{-W(\theta,x)}dx. \]

The strongly convex comparison \(V\) gives positive finite slice integrals and a Gaussian bound that is integrable in the latent variable, locally uniformly in the parameter. The displayed inequalities give positivity, finiteness, and decay of the original marginal as the parameter norm tends to infinity. Continuity of \(U\) and dominated convergence give continuity of that marginal. Its positivity, continuity, and decay then imply that it attains a maximum. Taking negative logarithms gives

\[ F_V(\theta)\le F_U(\theta)\le F_V(\theta)+\delta, \qquad F_W=-\log k_W. \]

Let \(\theta_U\) minimize \(F_U\) and let \(\theta_V\) minimize the \(m\)-strongly convex potential \(F_V\). The potential bounds and minimality give \(F_V(\theta_U)-F_V(\theta_V)\le\delta\). The quadratic-growth inequality therefore yields

\[ \frac m2\|\theta_U-\theta_V\|^2\le\delta. \]

In the equivalent notation \(V\le U\le V+\delta\), the pointwise weights satisfy \(e^{-\delta}e^{-V}\le e^{-U}\le e^{-V}\), and integration gives \(e^{-\delta}M_V(\theta)\le M_U(\theta)\le M_V(\theta)\). The positive finite comparison marginal makes \(M_U\) positive and finite. Thus logarithmic monotonicity legitimately yields \(F_V\le F_U\le F_V+\delta\) with \(F=-\log M\). The additive gap is still \(\delta\) because the logarithm is taken after integration. No differentiation of the original marginal or integration of an asymptotic remainder is used.

steps.title: The bound relative to the original marginal maximizer from finite displacement
steps.body:
The split Moreau gap is \(\delta=\lambda K^2/2\). Marginal integration and strong-convexity growth give

\[ \|\theta_\star-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\| \le\sqrt{\frac{\lambda K^2}{m}}. \]

Both marginal maximizers exist. Finite second moments justify Minkowski’s inequality in the form

\[ \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le\left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_{\lambda,\star}\|^2\right)^{1/2} +\|\theta_{\lambda,\star}-\theta_\star\|. \]

Insert the smoothed-model estimate and the deterministic displacement to obtain the stated bound relative to the original marginal maximizer. The square-root smoothing order is weaker than the source proposition’s claimed linear expansion. No parameter-fiber Hessian or uniform Taylor domination is assumed here, so the stronger order is not asserted.

sections.title: Full-potential smoothing and PIPULA
sections.intro: The full envelope of a strongly convex function has a reduced curvature, whereas adding a convex envelope to an unsmoothed strongly convex term preserves that term’s curvature. The full-envelope estimate below gives the constants needed for the qualified PIPULA conclusion.

steps.title: Strong convexity from the proximal minimizer comparison
steps.body:
Let \(U\) be \(m\)-strongly convex. Its full Moreau envelope is

\[ m_\lambda=\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\text{-strongly convex}. \]

Use the convex combination of the two proximal minimizers as a competitor. Strong convexity of \(U\) and the quadratic-combination identity give two nonnegative deficits. Their required bound is

\[ \frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|v\|^2 \le m\|u\|^2+\frac{\|u-v\|^2}{\lambda}. \]

The completed-square identity proves this coefficient without differentiability of \(U\). By comparison, smoothing only \(g_2\) and adding it to an unsmoothed strongly convex \(g_1\) preserves the curvature of the latter term.

In detail, put \(p=P_\lambda(x)\), \(q=P_\lambda(y)\), and \(z=ax+by\), and test at \(ap+bq\) for \(a+b=1\). The potential deficit is \(\frac{mab}{2}\|p-q\|^2\) and the penalty deficit is \(\frac{ab}{2\lambda}\|(p-q)-(x-y)\|^2\). Their sum is at least \(\frac{ab}{2}\frac{m}{1+m\lambda}\|x-y\|^2\) because \(\lambda(1+m\lambda)\) is positive. Equivalently, with \(u=p-q\) and \(v=x-y\), the two quadratic expressions are \(m\|u\|^2\) and \(\|u-v\|^2/\lambda\); their sum is bounded below by \(m\|v\|^2/(1+m\lambda)\). This is exactly the strong-convexity correction at the original inputs.

steps.title: The scope of the full-envelope PIPULA estimate
steps.body:
The specialization \(g_1=0\) and \(\lambda=\gamma\) identifies the update and its complete recursion with full-envelope IPLA. The source proximal deficit \(\mu\) gives strong-monotonicity constant \(\mu/\gamma\) because the residual is divided by \(\gamma\). A scale-uniform discretization theorem does not follow solely from the generic smoothness bound \(1/\gamma\).

The proved finite-time result assumes a finite bounded-below \(m\)-strongly convex full potential. For \(\gamma>0\) its full envelope has curvature \(m_\gamma=m/(1+m\gamma)\) and gradient constant \(1/\gamma\). The equal-scale step restriction holds automatically, so sharp concentration and Gaussian Euler transport give the estimate relative to the smoothed marginal maximizer. Its error term is \((33/20)(1/(\gamma m_\gamma))\sqrt{d_x+d_\theta/N}\sqrt\gamma\), diverging as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). This result consequently does not reproduce the source’s rate \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) relative to the original marginal maximizer; that rate requires additional analysis.

steps.title: The obstruction for a globally bounded proximal residual
steps.body:
Consider the reading of the source reduction in which \(g_1=0\) also applies the value-Lipschitz assumption to \(U=g_2\). Then \(U\) is globally \(K\)-Lipschitz, so its Moreau gradient \(R_\gamma=\gamma^{-1}(I-P_\gamma)\) satisfies \(\|R_\gamma(x)\|\le K\). A positive proximal deficit gives

\[ \frac{\mu}{\gamma}\|x-y\|^2 \le\langle x-y,R_\gamma(x)-R_\gamma(y)\rangle \le2K\|x-y\|. \]

The preceding obstruction contradicts these simultaneous global conditions on a nontrivial space. If the Lipschitz assumption instead concerns the nonsmooth term in an independent decomposition \(U=g_1+g_2\), it does not make the full \(U\) Lipschitz and the contradiction does not follow.

The residual \(R_\gamma=(I-P_\gamma)/\gamma\) is bounded in the first reading, while the deficit makes it strongly monotone with coefficient \(\mu/\gamma\). Under \(\mu>0\) these are incompatible. This is a conditional consistency result about the specified assumptions, not a general refutation of the source corollary. The separate full-potential PIPULA theorem assumes strong convexity and a lower bound without global value Lipschitzness.

sections.title: PIPGLA proximal energy inequalities
sections.intro: For each pair, proximal optimality gives a distance–energy inequality. Summation and Jensen’s inequality give the corresponding estimate for the averaged shared-parameter output. This valid inequality is used because that averaged output generally does not minimize a single proximal objective on the full state.

steps.title: The support and completed-square estimates
steps.body:
Let \(p=P_\lambda(y)\), \(s\in\partial g_2(y)\), and comparator \(a\) be given. The residual subgradient at \(p\) supplies a support evaluated at \(a\). Evaluate the support of \(s\) at \(p\) and combine the inequalities with the squared-distance expansion. Nonnegativity of \(\|(y-p)-\lambda s\|^2\) gives the inequality corresponding to Lemma A.8 of the source paper:

\[ \|p-a\|^2\le\|y-a\|^2 -2\lambda\bigl(g_2(y)-g_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2\|s\|^2. \]

Under \(\|s\|^2\le C\), the last term is at most \(\lambda^2C\). The selected minimal subgradient in the source assumption is one possible choice; any supporting subgradient with the same norm bound suffices.

In equivalent notation, put \(d=x-p\). The support at \(p\) gives \(2\eta[f(p)-f(a)]\le2\langle d,p-a\rangle\), and the input support gives \(f(x)-f(p)\le\langle s,d\rangle\). Their addition to the distance expansion leaves \(2\eta\langle s,d\rangle-\|d\|^2\le\eta^2\|s\|^2\), which follows from \(\|d-\eta s\|^2\ge0\). This proves the energy estimate directly from proximal optimality and the input subgradient bound.

steps.title: Summation of the pairwise proximal energy inequalities
steps.body:
The averaged pairwise output need not minimize the shared-state proximal objective. The valid comparison is instead

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_P(z)-a\|^2 \le\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|P(J_i z)-J_i a\|^2. \]

Apply the single-pair energy inequality to each term. The identities \(\sum_i\|J_i(z-a)\|^2=N\|z-a\|^2\) and \(G_2=N^{-1}\sum_i g_2\circ J_i\) give

\[ \|\operatorname{Pair}_{P_\lambda}(z)-a\|^2 \le\|z-a\|^2-2\lambda\bigl(G_2(z)-G_2(a)\bigr)+\lambda^2C. \]

This estimate uses the minimizing property only for each individual pair. It is the deterministic energy statement required in the splitting analysis; it is not by itself a stochastic convergence theorem.

A counterexample to shared-state proximal optimality has \(N=2\), \(g_2(\theta,x)=|\theta-x|\), proximal scale one, common parameter \(1\), and physical latent values \((0,4)\). The pair minimizers are \((1/2,1/2)\) and \((2,3)\), so averaging their parameter components gives \((5/4,1/2,3)\). The feasible shared-state competitor \((1,1,3)\) has objective \(3/2\), strictly below the pairwise output value \(51/32\).

To derive the valid estimate, apply the pair inequality at \(A_i z\) against \(A_i y\) and sum its \(N\) instances. The identity \(\sum_i\|A_i(z-y)\|^2=N\|z-y\|^2\) controls the initial squared distances. Divide by positive \(N\); the potential term becomes \(N^{-1}\sum_i[f(A_i z)-f(A_i y)]\). Equivalently the initial sum is \(N\|z-a\|^2\) and the potential sum is \(N[G_2(z)-G_2(a)]\), whose division by \(N>0\) gives the displayed full-state expression. Jensen supplies the parameter inequality, exact latent scaling supplies the other coordinates, and the averaged subgradient bounds supply the remainder.

steps.title: Common-innovation contraction of the splitting update
steps.body:
Jensen’s inequality for the common parameter and exact squared scaling of latent blocks make the averaged proximal map nonexpansive. Composing it with the smooth-gradient step, with the same innovation in both updates, gives

\[\|T_\gamma(z,\xi)-T_\gamma(w,\xi)\|\le(1-m\gamma)\|z-w\|.\]

Here the smooth part has curvature \(m\) and gradient constant \(L_1\) under \(0

sections.title: The stationary splitting comparison
sections.intro: Compare the splitting recursion with the stationary Langevin integral solution for the smoothed Gibbs potential. The Brownian construction gives stationarity, finite drift moments, and future-increment orthogonality. The energy comparison bounds an output coupling for each initial coupling, and its cost infimum gives the transport recurrence for the algorithm laws.

steps.title: Splitting laws and finite moments
steps.body:
Let \(T_\lambda\) be the averaged proximal map, \(F_1=\sum_i g_1(\theta,x_i)\) the smooth lifted potential, and \(h=\gamma/N\). The splitting recursion is

\[ X_{k+1}=T_\lambda\!\left(X_k-h\nabla F_1(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k\right). \]

Nonexpansiveness of \(T_\lambda\) and the Lipschitz smooth gradient imply continuity of the composed update and at most linear growth. Thus square-integrable inputs produce \(L^2\) iterates. Almost-sure representative equality identifies their laws with the pointwise recursion, giving probability normalization and finite moments before transport or real conversion.

An independent standard Gaussian sequence, independent of initialization, determines the joint input law. The measurable recursion therefore has the same finite-time distribution on every realization with that initial law and those innovation assumptions.

steps.title: Reference drift moments uniform in the envelope scale
steps.body:
Set \(f=\sum_i g_2(\theta,x_i)\) and \(e_\eta=\sum_i g_2^\eta(\theta,x_i)\). Pairwise value Lipschitzness, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the replicated-pair identity give

\[ \operatorname{Lip}(f),\operatorname{Lip}(e_\eta)\le NK, \qquad\|\nabla e_\eta\|\le NK, \qquad 0\le f-e_\eta\le \frac{N\eta K^2}{2}. \]

To preserve value Lipschitzness through the envelope, translate the old proximal minimizer by the input difference. Its quadratic penalty is unchanged, and the function increment is bounded by the original value constant. Differentiation then bounds the envelope-gradient magnitude. This is uniform in \(\eta>0\) despite the gradient-variation constant \(1/\eta\).

The strongly convex reference potential \(F_1+e_\eta\) has minimizer \(z_\eta\) satisfying \(\nabla F_1(z_\eta)=-\nabla e_\eta(z_\eta)\). Lipschitz growth of the smooth gradient with constant \(L\) and sharp Gibbs concentration give

\[ \mathbb E_\Pi\|\nabla F_1(Y)\|^2 \le \frac{2L^2D}{m_0}+2K_0^2, \]

Here \(m_0\) is the lifted curvature and \(K_0\) bounds \(\nabla e_\eta\). The total drift therefore has \(L^2\) norm at most \(G=\sqrt{2L^2D/m_0+2K_0^2}+K_0\). This magnitude estimate, rather than an inverse-scale gradient Lipschitz estimate, supplies the uniform reference moment used below.

steps.title: Expected orthogonality to future Brownian increments
steps.body:
An absolute Brownian norm bound would contribute order \(\sqrt h\) to the force pairing. Instead use the initialized Brownian past. The reference state at time \(t\) is measurable from initialization and the noise up to \(t\). Future increments are independent of that sigma-algebra and centered, so

\[ \mathbb E\left\langle\nabla e_\eta(Y_t), \sqrt2\,(B_h-B_t)\right\rangle=0, \qquad 0\le t\le h. \]

Full scalar-path independence and independent increments imply the grouped vector past–future independence. Almost-sure equality transfers these properties to the \(L^2\) representatives, and adaptedness of the integral solution makes its gradient observable past measurable. The expected inner product therefore vanishes by independence, with integrability supplied by the second moments.

steps.title: The local error decomposition and energy estimate
steps.body:
Let \(Y\) be a stationary reference with drift \(\nabla(F_1+e)\). Use its Brownian increment in the numerical forward state \(S=X-h\nabla F_1(X)+\sqrt2 B_h\) and define

\[ \begin{aligned} v&=(X-h\nabla F_1(X))-(Y_0-h\nabla F_1(Y_0)),\\ R&=\int_0^h[\nabla F_1(Y_t)-\nabla F_1(Y_0)]\,dt, & H&=\int_0^h\nabla e(Y_t)\,dt . \end{aligned} \]

The reference equation gives \(S-Y_h=v+R+H\). Apply the proximal energy inequality and retain the pairing with \(H\). Convex support bounds this pairing by expected envelope-energy differences; stationarity identifies the time-dependent reference values of \(e\) with their terminal value. Gap \(0\le f-e\le\delta\) contributes \(2h\delta\), and future-noise orthogonality leaves at most \(2h^2GK_0\). The smooth defect satisfies

\[ \|R\|_{L^2}\le Lh\bigl(Gh+\sqrt{2D}\sqrt h\bigr). \]

Weighted Young inequality and smooth contraction then give

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\|T(S)-Y_h\|^2 \le{}&(1-m_0h)\mathbb E\|X-Y_0\|^2+\mathcal B(h),\\ \mathcal B(h)={}&\left(1+\frac1{m_0h}\right) \left[Lh\bigl(Gh+\sqrt{2D}\sqrt h\bigr)\right]^2 +2h\delta+2h^2GK_0+h^2K_0^2. \end{aligned} \]

The reference stationarity, moments, and orthogonality are assumptions of this intermediate lemma and are established by the Brownian construction in the next argument. This is a synchronous mean-square proof of the recurrence, differing from the source’s heat-flow entropy proof.

steps.title: The stationary output coupling and transport infimum
steps.body:
Take any finite-cost coupling of current law \(\rho\) and smoothed Gibbs law \(\Pi\). Its product with the constructed Brownian probability space makes the noise independent of both initial coordinates. The reference starts at the second coordinate and remains Gibbs-stationary; its moments and expected future orthogonality follow from the integral construction.

The first coordinate’s forward update has the required independent Gaussian transition. The resulting output pair is a finite-cost coupling, to which the preceding energy estimate applies. Since its forcing is the same for every input coupling, the cost infimum gives

\[ W_2(\rho_{k+1},\Pi)^2 \le (1-m_0h)W_2(\rho_k,\Pi)^2+\mathcal B(h). \]

A single finite input coupling proves finite output transport. Taking all such costs gives the displayed recurrence without selecting an optimal coupling. This establishes the recurrence for the specified transition laws, in addition to the separate scalar summation result.

steps.title: The quadratic forcing and square-root transport error
steps.body:
Under \(0\[ C=\frac{4L^2}{m_0^2}\left(\frac{G^2}{m_0}+2D\right) +\frac{2}{m_0}\left(GK_0+K_0^2\right). \]

Expand the square of \(Gh+\sqrt{2D}\sqrt h\), use \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\), and bound the extra step factors by \(h\le1/m_0\). Summation of the contractive recurrence gives

\[ W_2(\rho_n,\Pi)^2 \le(1-m_0h)^n W_2(\rho_0,\Pi)^2+hC. \]

For the equal-scale particle algorithm set \(\eta=\lambda=\gamma\), \(h=\gamma/N\), \(m_0=Nm\), \(L=NL_1\), and \(K_0=NK\). The envelope gap is \(N\gamma K^2/2=hK_0^2/2\), which proves the forcing hypothesis. The reference is \(\Pi_{N,\gamma}\). Its moment coefficient \(G\) and resulting \(C_N\) are finite and independent of \(\gamma\). The transport error bound is therefore of order \(O(\sqrt\gamma)\) for fixed dimensions and particle count. The coefficient is conservative and differs from the source’s stated numerical forcing.

steps.title: The bound relative to the original marginal maximizer at positive proximal scales
steps.body:
The proximal parameter estimate is

\[ \|P_\lambda(x)-P_\eta(x)\|\le K|\lambda-\eta|. \]

Indeed let \(q=P_\eta(x)\) and \(s=(x-q)/\eta\). Optimality gives \(s\in\partial g_2(q)\) and \(\|s\|\le K\), so \(P_\lambda(q+\lambda s)=q\). Nonexpansiveness compares this shifted input with the original input. Jensen transfers the pair estimate with no extra factor of \(N\). Common-innovation contraction and the geometric sum then give separation at most \(K|\lambda-\eta|/(m\gamma)\) from identical initialization, which also bounds parameter root mean square separation.

Under the stated primitive assumptions, \(00\), and \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L_1)\), compare with the equal-step chain, project its transport bound, and add the finite center displacement. This yields

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\frac{K|\lambda-\gamma|}{m\gamma} +\sqrt{\frac{\gamma K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+\sqrt{(1-m\gamma)^n W_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\gamma})^2 +\frac{\gamma}{N}C_N}. \end{aligned} \]

The center \(\theta_\star\) maximizes the original nonsmooth marginal, and \(C_N\) is the preceding finite coefficient. Under interval condition \(\gamma\le\lambda\le\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\) and \(m\gamma<1\) the extra mismatch contribution is at most \(K\gamma/(1-m\gamma)\), including the upper scale. This estimate remains finite where the source’s scalar geometric denominator vanishes. It is a qualified version of the source theorem with square-root center displacement and different coupling constants. The source’s bounded-subgradient condition supplies value Lipschitzness by the supporting inequality.

sections.title: Conditional scalar recurrence estimates
sections.intro: Assume a real sequence satisfies the specified affine recurrence. The results in this section give its finite sum and distinguish strict geometric decay from the unit-ratio case. They do not identify an arbitrary such sequence with the transport error of a particle algorithm.

steps.title: The proposed coefficients and conditional finite sum
steps.body:
The source coefficients proposed for a squared transport error are

\[ q=\frac{\lambda(1-m\gamma)}\gamma, \qquad b=\lambda\left(\frac{2\gamma L_1D}{N}+\lambda C\right), \quad D=d_\theta+Nd_x. \]

Only the Gaussian contribution is divided by \(N\). Multiplication of a gradient by \(N\) multiplies its squared norm by \(N^2\). Version 3 includes \(\lambda NC\) before cancellation and has this scaling correctly; the algebraic comparison concerns the earlier version.

Assume \(0\le q\) and \(e_{n+1}\le q e_n+b\). Nonnegative multiplication and induction give

\[ e_n\le q^n e_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j. \]

For \(0\le q<1\) the finite sum equals \(e_n\le q^n e_0+b(1-q^n)/(1-q)\). If \(b\) is nonnegative, its negative tail may be discarded, giving error term \(b/(1-q)\). These statements retain the recurrence as a hypothesis and do not by themselves establish it for the algorithm.

steps.title: The strict geometric regime and unit ratio
steps.body:
Under \(0\[ \lambda<\frac\gamma{1-m\gamma}. \]

The source allows equality at the upper scale in the cited corollaries and theorem. At that scale \(q=1\), so its geometric denominator vanishes. The finite recurrence instead gives \(e_n\le e_0+nb\), without a bounded geometric error term.

Positive step and denominator conditions justify the strict-regime division. Under \(\lambda=\gamma\) the scalar expression is \(\gamma(2L_1D/N+C)/m\). This is a consequence of the assumed recurrence, separate from the transport recurrence derived by the stationary splitting argument.

sections.title: The finite-particle MYPGD estimate
sections.intro: MYPGD uses latent Langevin innovations and omits the common parameter innovation. An exact common-noise comparison with MYIPLA gives a finite-particle transport bound and, after projection, a parameter-error bound. No mean-field convergence premise is required for that comparison.

steps.title: Parameter projection and the exact noise variance
steps.body:
Let \(P_\theta\) project onto the parameter coordinates and \(P_x=I-P_\theta\) onto the latent coordinates. Both are bounded orthogonal linear maps. For standard Gaussian \(\xi\), coordinate means and variances give

\[ \mathbb E[P_\theta\xi]=0, \qquad \mathbb E\|P_\theta\xi\|^2=d_\theta. \]

For square-integrable \(A\) independent of \(\xi\), Cauchy–Schwarz makes the mixed term integrable. Expansion and factorization of its expectation give

\[ \mathbb E\|A+aP_\theta\xi\|^2 =\mathbb E\|A\|^2+a^2d_\theta. \]

The mean-zero projected Gaussian makes the mixed expectation vanish. Thus removal of the parameter noise changes the squared coupling cost by its exact variance, without the loss from a triangle bound.

steps.title: The common deterministic smoothed gradient map
steps.body:
Let \(F_\eta=\sum_i(g_1+g_2^\eta)( heta,x_i)\) and \(h=\gamma/N\). The residual-envelope identity gives the update

\[ X_{k+1}=X_k-h abla F_\eta(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,P_x\xi_k. \]

The parameter coordinate has no additive Gaussian term, while each physical latent coordinate has coefficient \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). Finite-second-moment initialization and independent standard Gaussian coordinates, independent of initialization, define the transition laws. The unused parameter Gaussians may remain on the probability space for comparison with MYIPLA; no initial independent-particle assumption is required.

The bound \(\operatorname{Lip}(I-(\gamma/N) abla F_\eta)\le1+|\gamma/N|\,NL_\eta\) ensures continuity and measurable finite-moment updates without imposing contraction. In particular the deterministic map is \(D(z)=z-(\gamma/N) abla F_\eta(z)\), and the physical latent noise coefficient is \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). The stricter step restriction is required only for the quantitative contractive comparison.

steps.title: Contraction of the smoothed gradient step
steps.body:
The smoothed gradient step contracts by \(r=1-m\gamma\) under \(0\[ W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_{k+1},\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_{k+1})^2 \le r^2 W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_k,\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_k)^2 +\frac{2\gamma d_\theta}{N}. \]

Take the input coupling infimum at each step. From the same initial law, \(0\le r<1\) and \(1-r^2=m\gamma(2-m\gamma)\ge m\gamma\) give

\[ W_2(\rho^{\mathrm{PGD}}_n,\rho^{\mathrm{IPLA}}_n)^2 \le\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}. \]

For \(V_\eta=g_1+g_2^\eta\), the envelope results give curvature \(m\) and gradient constant \(L_\eta=L_1+\eta^{-1}\). Lifting gives \(Nm,NL_\eta\), so the step \(\gamma/N\) has contraction \(r=1-m\gamma\). Restriction \(0<\gamma\le2/(m+L_\eta)\) and \(m\le L_\eta\) imply \(0\le m\gamma\le1\) and thus \(0\le r<1\).

With \(r=1-m\gamma\) and \(a^2=2\gamma/N\), the denominator in the geometric sum is \(1-r^2=m\gamma(2-m\gamma)\). Inequality \(m\gamma\le1\) bounds it below by \(m\gamma>0\). Cancellation of the physical step gives the squared radius \(2d_\theta/(Nm)\). This is an upper bound on the difference between two finite-particle laws. It asserts neither that removing noise worsens the algorithm nor that a mean-field limit has been taken.

steps.title: The MYPGD bound about the original marginal maximizer
steps.body:
Apply the projected transport inequality to the two algorithm laws and substitute the MYIPLA estimate relative to the original marginal maximizer. With \(L_\eta=L_1+1/\eta\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \left(\mathbb E\|\theta^{\mathrm{PGD}}_n-\theta_\star\|^2\right)^{1/2} \le{}&\sqrt{\frac{2d_\theta}{Nm}} +\sqrt{\frac{\eta K^2}{m}}+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\\ &+(1-m\gamma)^nW_2(\rho_0,\Pi_{N,\eta})\\ &+\frac{33}{20}\frac{L_\eta}{m} \sqrt{d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}}\sqrt\gamma. \end{aligned} \]

The result is finite under the stated assumptions. It is a finite-particle version related to the source’s Appendix B theorem: its initial transient is measured from the smoothed Gibbs target and it adds a conservative noise-comparison radius. It does not reproduce the source’s mean-field metric, constants, or stronger Taylor smoothing claim. The remaining discretization coefficient contains \(L_1+1/\eta\). Thus the estimate retains its dependence on smoothing scale and does not assert a bound for a path supremum.

sections.title: Mean-field equations and smoothing and sampling estimates
sections.intro: The potential gradient and a bounded parameter-averaging operator define the mean-field drift on the Hilbert space of square-integrable states. Picard gives its finite-horizon integral solution. Gradient comparison gives a smoothing estimate, and independent sample variance supplies the particle forcing. These mean-square conclusions do not alone imply pathwise stochastic-equation or partial-differential-equation statements.

steps.title: Separate parameter and probability-law perturbations
steps.body:
For differentiable \(V\) define

\[ b_V( heta,\mu)=\int abla_ heta V( heta,x)\,\mu(dx). \]

Assume \( abla V\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(\mu, u\) have finite second moments. Linear growth gives integrability. Comparison on a finite-cost coupling, Cauchy–Schwarz, and the cost infimum then give

\[ \|b_V( heta,\mu)-b_V( heta', u)\| \le L igl(\| heta- heta'\|+W_2(\mu, u) igr). \]

For split envelope \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\) the gradient constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\). The source’s \(1/\eta\) constant is the full-envelope constant and is not in general sufficient for this split potential. Moreover the present estimate is in quadratic Wasserstein distance, a weaker conclusion than the source’s first-Wasserstein assertion. It does not alone establish the later propositions cited there.

For arbitrary coupling \((X,Y)\), the \(L\)-Lipschitz joint gradient gives \(\| abla_ heta U( heta,x)- abla_ heta U(\vartheta,y)\|\le L(\| heta-\vartheta\|+\|x-y\|)\). Integration and Cauchy–Schwarz on \(\mathbb E\|X-Y\|\) yield

\[\|b( heta,\mu)-b(\vartheta, u)\|\le L\| heta-\vartheta\|+LW_2(\mu, u).\]

The Moreau substitution gives \(L_1+\eta^{-1}\). Alternatively insert intermediate force \(b_V( heta',\mu)\): its parameter change is at most \(L\| heta- heta'\|\) and its law change at most \(LW_2(\mu, u)\). Their sum proves the claim with constant \(L_1+1/\eta\) for split smoothing.

steps.title: The mean-field integral equation and its parameter and latent components
steps.body:
On the Hilbert space of square-integrable joint vectors define

\[ \mathcal A_V(X)(\omega)= \begin{pmatrix} \mathbb E\nabla_\theta V(X)\\ \nabla_x V(X(\omega)) \end{pmatrix}. \]

Expectation and coordinate projections are contractions. The averaging operator has sufficient norm bound two, so \(\nabla V\) being \(L\)-Lipschitz gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_V)\le2L\). Picard’s theorem yields a continuous square-integrable solution on any finite horizon:

\[ Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal A_V(Y_s)\,ds+B_t^x. \]

Take deterministic initial parameter \(\theta_0\), square-integrable latent initialization, and a Brownian input projected onto the latent coordinates. Its mean-square continuity and zero initial value follow from the Brownian second moments. Parameter projection of the equation is constant as a random vector, giving deterministic continuous path \(\theta_t\). With latent component \(X_t\) and law \(\mu_t\), the projected equations are

\[ \begin{aligned} \theta_t&=\theta_0-\int_0^t\int \nabla_\theta V(\theta_s,x)\,\mu_s(dx)\,ds,\\ X_t-X_0&=-\int_0^t\nabla_xV(\theta_s,X_s)\,ds+\sqrt2 B_t. \end{aligned} \]

For \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\) the gradient constant is \(L_1+1/\eta\) by the Moreau estimates. The conclusion is mean-square integral existence and the two displayed identities. It does not separately prove a continuous pathwise strong stochastic equation, adaptedness, or a Fokker–Planck or gradient-flow partial differential equation.

steps.title: The finite smoothing estimate for the two integral systems
steps.body:
Assume \(g_2\) is differentiable with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz gradient, and retain convexity, a lower bound, and value Lipschitz constant \(K\). The supporting residual equals the gradient at the proximal minimizer:

\[ \nabla g_2^\eta(v)=\nabla g_2(P_\eta(v)). \]

Nonexpansiveness of \(P_\eta\) preserves constant \(L_2\), and \(\|v-P_\eta(v)\|\le\eta K\) gives

\[ \|\nabla g_2(v)-\nabla g_2^\eta(v)\|\le\eta L_2K. \]

If instead regularity is stated for \(U=g_1+g_2\) with constant \(L_U\) and for \(g_1\) with constant \(L_1\), the difference argument supplies \(L_2=L_U+L_1\).

Construct both Hilbert-space solutions with common initial state and continuous additive input. The averaged drifts differ uniformly by at most \(2\eta L_2K\). Their pair-gradient constant is at most \(L_1+L_2\), independent of \(\eta\). The averaging operator gives the corresponding factor two. Grönwall yields

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\|Y_t-Z_t\|_{L^2} \le 2\eta L_2K\,\Psi(2(L_1+L_2),T), \qquad \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0.\end{cases} \]

For deterministic initial parameter and latent-only Brownian input these are the mean-field systems described above. The finite bound is linear in \(\eta\). More explicitly the averaged drift constant is \(2(L_1+L_2)\) and its uniform difference is \(2\eta L_2K\). The supremum is outside the \(L^2\) norm. Proposition C.3 instead bounds the expectation of the supremum of squared errors. The square root of that quantity bounds the supremum of the L² error norms. A bound on the expectation of the supremum of squared errors is not established here.

steps.title: The variance of an independent sample mean
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\) and let \(\phi\) be square-integrable under probability \(\mu\). On \(\mu^{\otimes N}\) the coordinate samples are independent. Center \(\phi\) by its expectation, expand the squared sample mean, and cancel its off-diagonal pairings. This gives

\[ \mathbb E_{\mu^{\otimes N}} \left\|\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\right\|^2 =\frac1N\mathbb E_\mu\|\phi-\mathbb E_\mu\phi\|^2. \]

The root mean square sampling factor is \(N^{-1/2}\). This variance identity is an ingredient in particle comparison, not by itself a propagation-of-chaos theorem. Exchangeability alone would not cancel covariances.

Indeed let \(C_i=\phi(X_i)-\mathbb E\phi\). Its average is \(N^{-1}\sum_iC_i\), the expected squared sum is \(N\mathbb E\|C_1\|^2\), and the averaging prefactor is \(N^{-2}\). Their product is \(N^{-1}\mathbb E\|C_1\|^2\). Taking square roots gives \(1/\sqrt N\). Independence here comes from the finite product construction, rather than an assumption about interacting particle states.

sections.title: Independent-copy particle comparison and tagged laws
sections.intro: Construct one mean-field reference and, for every positive particle count, the empirical-gradient particle equation with independent copied initialization. The horizon coefficient is chosen from the reference before particle count varies. The conclusion is uniform over time after taking the mean-square norm. Proposition C.2, equation (45), bounds \(\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}(\|\Delta\theta_t\|+\|\Delta X_t\|)\). Here the bound concerns \(\sup_{t\le T}(\mathbb E[\|\Delta\theta_t\|^2+\|\Delta X_t\|^2])^{1/2}\). These two quantities are not generally ordered. The source conclusion is not asserted by this theorem.

steps.title: The physical particle drift and its integral equation
steps.body:
Assume differentiable \(V\) has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, latent probability \(\mu\) has finite second moment, and parameter \(\theta_0\) is deterministic. Fix \(T\ge0\). Use the physical coordinate space

\[ H_N=L^2(\Theta)\times\prod_{i=1}^N L^2(X_i),\qquad \|Z\|_{H_N}=\max\{\|\Theta\|_2,\max_i\|X_i\|_2\}. \]

Define its empirical-gradient drift by

\[ \mathcal A_N(Z)=\left(\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\nabla_\theta V(\Theta,X_i), (\nabla_xV(\Theta,X_i))_{i=1}^N\right). \]

The reconstruction inequality \(\|(\Delta\Theta,\Delta X_i)\|_2\le\|\Delta\Theta\|_2+\|\Delta X_i\|_2\) and gradient Lipschitzness give \(\operatorname{Lip}(\mathcal A_N)\le2L\) independently of \(N>0\). Each coordinate is bounded by the maximum norm; averaging parameter forces and taking the latent maximum introduce no particle factor. Completeness and Picard give the finite-horizon continuous mean-square solution. The drift remains the empirical particle force, rather than a substituted expectation.

steps.title: Independent reference copies and the exact parameter residual
steps.body:
Let \(Y_t=(\theta_t,X_t)\) be the reference on probability space \(Q\). On \(Q^{\otimes N}\) use coordinate pullbacks for its independent latent copies while retaining deterministic parameter \(\theta_t\). These pullbacks and the reference-state assembly are bounded linear maps, so they commute with the time integral and give the copied reference equation.

The latent drifts agree with the particle drifts. Their only discrepancy is the parameter empirical mean:

\[ \delta_N(t)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\nabla_\theta V(\theta_t,X_t^i) -\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(\theta_t,X_t),\qquad \|\delta_N(t)\|_2= \frac{\|\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)-\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)\|_2}{\sqrt N}. \]

The norm equality follows by expanding the centered squared sample mean; all mixed expectations vanish under the product law. Thus independence is constructed, and is not inferred from exchangeability of interacting states.

steps.title: The prescribed initialization and Brownian particle inputs
steps.body:
Take the product of latent law \(\mu\) and the constructed joint Brownian probability space. Initial pair \((\theta_0,X_0)\) has latent law \(\mu\) and finite second moment, independent of the full Brownian family. On \(Q^{\otimes N}\) select each particle’s latent coordinates from its own source copy and the parameter coordinates from row zero. Distinct coordinate tags make the complete selection injective and jointly independent.

The resulting equations are

\[ \begin{aligned} \Theta_t^N-\theta_0&=-\int_0^t\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_\theta V(\Theta_s^N,X_s^{i,N})\,ds+\sqrt{2/N}\,B_t^\theta,\\ X_t^{i,N}-X_0^i&=-\int_0^t\nabla_xV(\Theta_s^N,X_s^{i,N})\,ds+\sqrt2 B_t^{x,i}. \end{aligned} \]

The parameter Brownian input has exact mean-square norm \(\sqrt{2d_\theta t/N}\). On \([0,T]\) this is at most \(b/\sqrt N\) with \(b=\sqrt{2d_\theta}\sqrt T\). The increment second moments also prove continuity and zero initial value, supplying the additive-input hypotheses for the particle equation.

steps.title: A particle-count-independent finite-horizon comparison constant
steps.body:
The centered reference force is continuous in mean square. Compactness of \([0,T]\) therefore gives finite \(C\ge0\) satisfying

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\| \nabla_\theta V(Y_t)-\mathbb E_Q\nabla_\theta V(Y_t)\|_2\le C. \]

The constant \(C\) is chosen from the reference potential, initial law, and horizon, before \(N\) varies. Subtract the two integral equations and then the extra parameter Brownian input. The remaining difference is a time integral to which Grönwall applies. Put

\[ \Psi(a,T)=\begin{cases}(e^{aT}-1)/a,&a>0,\\T,&a=0,\end{cases} \qquad C_T=2\big[(C+2Lb)\Psi(2L,T)+b\big]. \]

For every \(N>0\) this constructs the particle integral solution with independent copied initialization and, for every \(i\), gives

\[ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\left( \|\Theta_t^N-\theta_t\|_2+\|X_t^{i,N}-X_t^i\|_2\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N}. \]

For \(V=g_1+g_2^\eta\) use \(L=L_1+1/\eta\); the coefficient may depend on \(\eta\). The estimate is uniform after taking each mean-square norm. Proposition C.2, equation (45), bounds the expectation of the supremum of unsquared errors. That quantity and the supremum of the L² error norms are not generally ordered. This proof does not interchange supremum and expectation.

steps.title: The tagged one-time Wasserstein estimate
steps.body:
The tagged pair \((\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N})\) and the corresponding copy of \(Y_t=(\theta_t,X_t)\) have finite second moments on the same probability space. Coordinate evaluation preserves the reference law, so their joint distribution is a coupling of the required marginals. The pair norm is at most the sum of coordinate norms; Minkowski and the coordinate comparison give

\[ W_2\!\left(\mathcal L(\Theta_t^N,X_t^{i,N}),\mathcal L(\theta_t,X_t)\right) \le\frac{C_T}{\sqrt N},\qquad 0\le t\le T. \]

The conclusion retains the empirical-gradient particle integral equation, independent copied initial law, and specified Brownian input. One finite coupling proves transport finiteness before real conversion. The bound concerns one-time tagged laws; the source’s pathwise stochastic-equation, expected path-supremum, and partial-differential-equation statements are not asserted.

sections.title: Corrections and remaining source claims
sections.intro: The comparison records each source statement with its proved scope. Page numbers refer to version 3. A qualified version may have different constants, assumptions, or norms; a result listed as unproved is not claimed to follow from the present arguments.

steps.title: The second-order sign in the quadratic proximal expansion
steps.body:
The proximal equation \(p+\lambda\nabla g_2(p)=x\) gives a positive second-order coefficient in the scalar quadratic example:

\[ \operatorname{prox}_{u^2/2}^\lambda(x) =\frac{x}{1+\lambda} =x-\lambda x+\lambda^2x-\frac{\lambda^3x}{1+\lambda}. \]

The negative coefficient printed in the source leaves error at least \(\lambda^2\) at \(x=1\) and therefore cannot be its third-order expansion. The quadratic is not globally value Lipschitz, so this calculation diagnoses the displayed algebra rather than refuting a full theorem under that assumption.

Almost-everywhere twice differentiability and the stated moment condition also do not provide the uniform integrable third-order remainder needed for the claimed order \(O(\lambda)\) for displacement of the original marginal maximizer. The proved finite-gap result gives \(\sqrt{\lambda K^2/m}\); this difference in established scope does not prove the stronger assertion false. For \(f(u)=u^2/2\) the minimizer equation is \((1+\lambda)p=x\). Division gives the exact resolvent and its positive \(\lambda^2x\) term with the displayed third-order remainder.

steps.title: The scope of each source-theorem comparison
steps.body:
MYIPLA. The theorem relative to the original marginal maximizer retains explicit \(L_1+1/\lambda\) dependence, sharp second-moment factor \(d_\theta/(Nm)\), and the discrete transient. The finite smoothing term has square-root order. The source’s linear Taylor expression and its precise strong-stochastic-equation formulation are not separately proved, although the stationary comparison integral process is constructed.

PIPGLA. The result relative to the original marginal maximizer follows from the pairwise proximal energy inequality, Jensen, and a stationary synchronous Brownian coupling. The finite coefficient is independent of the forward step; parameter sensitivity covers all positive proximal scales with its mismatch term. These constants differ from the source. The exact heat-flow entropy argument and its printed numerical corollaries are not established by this different proof.
